(CNN) -- Investigators are pursuing several new leads in the case of a missing 5-year-old girl in Florida, they said Tuesday. Haleigh Ann-Marie Cummings, 5, who vanished a week ago, may have been abducted, police say. The Putnam County Sheriff's Office on Monday night searched the neighborhood of Haleigh Ann-Marie Cummings, who vanished a week ago. Deputies also searched surrounding neighborhoods. Authorities said the girl may have been abducted. Officials wouldn't release any details on the leads. "Those leads, like I said, are as a result of doing the neighborhood canvass last night, and we will be following up on those leads today," said Capt. Steve Rose of the Putnam Sheriff's Office. Since opening the case a week ago, authorities have received more than 1,200 tips about the missing girl, 500 of them since Monday, Putnam County Sheriff Rick Ryan said. Tuesday afternoon, the sheriff's office announced they have changed the Amber Alert they originally put out for the little girl, saying they changed the description of the clothing. "What we need people to focus on is the face, because we do not know at this time what the clothing was at this point," said Dominick Pape with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Rose said investigators also conducted a checkpoint in the area last night. Ronald Cummings' girlfriend, 17-year-old Misty Croslin, told police she was watching Haleigh when she went missing sometime before dawn February 10.  Watch why police now question the sitter's story » . Cummings shares his double-wide mobile home with Croslin, daughter Haleigh and a 4-year-old son in Satsuma, east of Gainesville. He has said that when he returned home at 3 a.m. ET, he was surprised to see Croslin awake and asked her why she was up. Croslin waited until Cummings came home to phone 911 about the girl's disappearance, though it's unclear how long that wait was, authorities said. Police said last week that Croslin had tucked the girl and her brother into bed at 8 p.m. before going to sleep at 10. The girl, boy and Croslin usually sleep in the same bed. Officials said they originally thought Haleigh may have wandered outside on her own but are now certain that she was abducted. Investigators are looking into various angles of the case, including finding out the location of 44 registered sexual offenders who live within a 5-mile radius of the Cummings home, said Lt. Johnny Greenwood of the Putnam Sheriff's Office. A nationwide Amber Alert said the girl was last seen wearing a pink shirt and underwear.

(CNN) — Investigators are pursuing several new leads in the case of a missing 5-year-old Florida girl who may have been abducted, authorities said Tuesday.

Haleigh Ann-Marie Cummings vanished a week ago. On Monday night, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office searched her neighborhood, as well as surrounding communities. Officials declined to release details about the new leads.

“Those leads, like I said, are as a result of doing the neighborhood canvass last night, and we will be following up on those leads today,” said Capt. Steve Rose of the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office.

Since the case was opened a week ago, authorities have received more than 1,200 tips about the missing girl, including 500 since Monday, Putnam County Sheriff Rick Ryan said.

On Tuesday afternoon, the sheriff’s office announced that it had revised the Amber Alert originally issued for Haleigh, changing the description of her clothing.

“What we need people to focus on is the face, because we do not know at this time what the clothing was at this point,” said Dominick Pape of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Rose said investigators also conducted a checkpoint in the area Monday night.

Ronald Cummings’ girlfriend, 17-year-old Misty Croslin, told police she was watching Haleigh when the girl disappeared sometime before dawn on February 10. Watch why police now question the sitter’s story »

Cummings shares his double-wide mobile home in Satsuma, east of Gainesville, with Croslin, his daughter Haleigh and his 4-year-old son. He has said that when he returned home at 3 a.m. ET, he was surprised to find Croslin awake and asked her why she was up.

Croslin waited until Cummings returned home before calling 911 to report the girl’s disappearance, although authorities said it remains unclear how long she waited.

Police said last week that Croslin had tucked Haleigh and her brother into bed at 8 p.m. before going to sleep at 10 p.m. The girl, her brother and Croslin usually sleep in the same bed.

Officials said they initially believed Haleigh might have wandered outside on her own but are now certain she was abducted.

Investigators are examining various aspects of the case, including determining the whereabouts of 44 registered sex offenders who live within a 5-mile radius of the Cummings home, said Lt. Johnny Greenwood of the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office.

A nationwide Amber Alert said Haleigh was last seen wearing a pink shirt and underwear.

Haleigh was reported missing from a mobile home in Satsuma, about 60 miles south of Jacksonville, in February 2009. Despite extensive searches, thousands of tips and national attention, she has never been found.

Authorities have not publicly disclosed the nature of the latest leads, citing the active investigation. Detectives are reviewing earlier statements, reexamining evidence and following up on information received since the girl disappeared.

**Florida girl’s disappearance investigated as suspected abduction**

**SATSUMA, Fla. —** Five-year-old Haleigh Cummings vanished from her family’s mobile home in Putnam County during the early hours of Feb. 10, 2009, prompting an extensive search and an investigation that authorities later classified as an abduction.

Haleigh was last seen the previous evening at the home on Green Lane in Satsuma, about 60 miles south of Jacksonville. Her father, Ronald Cummings, was working overnight, and his girlfriend, Misty Croslin, was caring for Haleigh and her younger brother.

Croslin told investigators she put the children to bed and awoke at about 3 a.m. to find Haleigh missing. The home’s rear door was open, and a concrete block—normally used as a step—had been moved and was holding the door open.

“The probability of her wandering off is very slim,” Putnam County Sheriff’s Office spokesman Lt. Johnny Greenwood told reporters during the initial investigation. Authorities said Haleigh would have had difficulty moving the block herself.

Law-enforcement officers, firefighters and volunteers searched woods, waterways and nearby properties. Divers examined ponds and sections of the St. Johns River, while investigators conducted interviews and followed hundreds of tips. An Amber Alert described Haleigh as 3 feet tall, weighing about 39 pounds, with blond hair and brown eyes.

Investigators found no clear evidence of forced entry. Nevertheless, Sheriff Jeff Hardy later said the case had been formally classified as an abduction. In 2010, after another intensive search, Hardy announced that investigators believed Haleigh was “most likely deceased” and that her death was probably the result of foul play.

Authorities identified no charged suspect in Haleigh’s disappearance. They also cautioned that inconsistencies in witness accounts did not by themselves establish criminal responsibility.

Haleigh has never been found, and the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office continues to list the case as an active missing-child investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact the sheriff’s office or the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

## Florida Police Say Missing 5-Year-Old Was Likely Abducted as New Leads Emerge

Florida investigators now believe 5-year-old Haleigh Cummings was taken from her home rather than wandering away on her own, marking an important shift in the search for the missing Putnam County girl.

Haleigh disappeared during the night of Feb. 9, 2009, from the Satsuma mobile home she shared with her father, Ronald Cummings. Her father was at work, and his girlfriend, Misty Croslin, was caring for Haleigh and her younger brother.

Croslin told investigators she put the children to bed and later discovered Haleigh missing. A rear door was reportedly open, and Croslin said it had been secured before she went to sleep.

### Why investigators doubt Haleigh wandered away

Authorities initially considered several possibilities, including that Haleigh had left the house by herself. Search teams, police dogs, divers and volunteers combed nearby woods, roads and waterways without finding evidence that she had become lost.

Investigators now say the circumstances make that explanation increasingly unlikely. Haleigh had a medical condition that affected her mobility, making it difficult for her to travel far without assistance. Search dogs also failed to establish a convincing trail showing that she walked away from the home.

The lack of physical evidence in the heavily searched area, combined with questions about how the rear door was opened, has led detectives to focus on the possibility that another person removed her from the residence.

Police have not publicly identified a suspect or explained whether they believe Haleigh was taken by someone she knew. They have emphasized that the abduction theory is based on the totality of the evidence rather than a single discovery.

### New leads draw scrutiny to people close to the case

The investigation has increasingly centered on conflicting accounts from people who were in or around the home before Haleigh vanished. Detectives have repeatedly interviewed Croslin and examined discrepancies in the timeline she provided.

Investigators have also pursued information involving Croslin’s brother, Hank “Tommy” Croslin Jr., and a cousin, Joe Overstreet. At one stage, a tip connected to people in Haleigh’s family circle prompted an extensive search of the St. Johns River near Satsuma. Divers and law-enforcement officers examined the water and shoreline for evidence.

Reports surrounding that lead suggested investigators were considering whether Haleigh’s disappearance followed a confrontation or an attempted theft at the Cummings home. Overstreet denied involvement, and authorities did not announce that the river search had produced Haleigh’s remains or conclusive proof of what happened.

Police have also reviewed phone records, re-interviewed witnesses and checked tips involving vehicles or unfamiliar people seen in the neighborhood. Known offenders in the area were examined early in the case, but officials have not disclosed evidence publicly linking any of them to Haleigh’s disappearance.

### Case remains unresolved

The shift toward an abduction theory does not mean investigators have determined who took Haleigh or whether she is still alive. No one has been charged in connection with her disappearance, and several of the most publicized leads remain unproven.

Authorities continue to describe the case as active and have urged anyone with firsthand information to contact law enforcement. Investigators say even a detail that once appeared insignificant could help establish who was at the home, how Haleigh was removed and where she was taken.
